sections.markdown:
## C — Regulatory, railroad, work zone and guide signs: stop, yield, wrong way and lane control signs, speed limits and minimums, railroad crossing duties, work zone types and fines, guide and service signs, route and exit numbering, and reference markers
Knowledge domain: what stop, yield, wrong way, do not enter, one way, lane control and keep right signs require, how posted and default speed limits work, what to do at railroad crossings, how to drive through each type of work zone, what guide, service and route signs show, how interstate and exit numbers are assigned, and what emergency reference markers tell you. Pictures in these pages are not described; only their written meanings are used.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
A stop sign is an eight-sided red sign with white letters, and it requires a full stop and a wait until crossing traffic and pedestrians have cleared. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
Stop at the stop line when there is one, even if it is beyond the sign; without a line, stop near the edge of the intersection, look both ways and go when safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
The stopping point order is the stop line first, then the crosswalk if there is no line, and otherwise just before entering the intersection. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
A yield sign is a red and white triangle with red letters that means slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic in the intersection or road you are joining. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
A Wrong Way sign means you turned into a lane of oncoming traffic, so pull off, turn around and go back as quickly and safely as you can. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
A Do Not Enter sign at a road opening means you may not drive into that road, and a One Way sign means traffic there moves in a single direction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A01
Lane control signs, posted beside or above the road, use arrows to show which way each lane may go. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A02
A speed limit sign shows the legal maximum under ideal conditions, and the law requires you to slow down when hills, curves, slick roads, short sight lines, pedestrians, cyclists or slow vehicles make that speed unsafe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A02
Interstates also have minimum speeds, and under normal conditions you may not drive slower than 40 mph on an interstate; if that is too fast for you, use another route. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A02
A Keep Right sign means traffic must pass only on the right side of a feature or obstruction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A02
Inside a city, town or village the speed limit is 25 mph whenever no other limit is posted. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A02
The Missouri Highway and Transportation Commission may set limits above or below the uniform maximums for safety or to keep traffic moving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
The guide's default maximum for rural expressways is 65 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
The guide's default maximum is 60 mph both for interstates, freeways and expressways inside urbanized areas and for other roads outside urbanized areas. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A02
Lettered roads have a default maximum speed of 55 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A02
A round advance warning sign, and in some places a pavement marking, tells you a railroad crossing is ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A02
Never race a train to a crossing, and never start across the tracks until there is room for your whole vehicle on the far side. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A02
Avoid shifting gears while crossing railroad tracks in case the vehicle stalls. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A03
The white X-shaped crossbuck at a crossing means the same as a yield sign, so you must yield to trains, and a sign beneath it gives the number of tracks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A03
Where a crossing has alternately flashing red lights or a lowering gate, you must stop and stay stopped until the train has passed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A03
When the red lights flash or the gate is down, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest track, and never drive around the gate. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A03
Crossing lights may keep flashing after a train clears, and where there are two or more tracks, check for a second train before crossing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A03
Work zone signs are fluorescent orange, and flaggers or other devices may guide you through the work area. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A03
On Missouri state roads, a driver caught speeding or passing in a work zone faces a minimum fine of $250 the first time and $300 for each repeat, plus any other lawful fines. [A03]
Why it matters: dynamic detail: statutory amounts can change.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A04
In any work zone, stay alert for lower speed limits, narrow lanes and workers, avoid distractions, obey the signs and watch for vehicles moving in and out. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A04
For a shoulder work zone, where the work is on or past the shoulder, reduce speed as you approach. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A04
For a lane closure, merge into the marked open lane and slow to the posted work zone speed limit. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A05
A flagging operation closes one lane of a two-lane, two-way road, with flaggers at each end, so be ready to stop and follow their directions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A05
In a mobile work zone, slow or stopped work vehicles move along a travel lane and workers may step out, so expect them near the road. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A05
Approaching a mobile work zone, look for a protective vehicle in the lane with a flashing arrow panel showing which lane to merge into, often signed Slow Vehicles. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A06
Guide signs are green or brown squares or rectangles with white letters showing direction and distance to cities, airports and state lines or to parks, historic sites and museums. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A06
Service signs are blue squares or rectangles with white letters or symbols marking services such as rest areas and hospitals. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A06
The shape of a route sign tells you the road type, whether interstate, United States, state or county. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A06
Routes running north and south carry odd numbers, and routes running east and west carry even numbers. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A06
A three-digit interstate number starting with an even digit, such as I-270 or I-435, loops around a city, while one starting with an odd digit, such as I-155 or I-170, is a spur into a city. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F36 | anchor: A06
Exit numbers on east-west interstates start at zero in the west and rise heading east, and on north-south interstates they start in the south and rise heading north. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec09-F37 | anchor: A06
Emergency reference markers along the outside shoulder mark the road edge and show direction and route number, and they are spaced every two-tenths of a mile so one is always in view. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0056]

Misconceptions: a posted speed limit is not a safe speed in every condition, and the law requires slowing when conditions demand it; a crossbuck alone means yield, but flashing lights or a lowered gate mean stop; driving very slowly on an interstate is not automatically legal; a stop line placed past the sign is still where you stop.
Mnemonics: odd goes up and down the map, even goes across; even first digit goes around the city, odd first digit goes into it.
Glossary: crossbuck means the white X-shaped sign at a railroad crossing; lane control sign means an arrow sign assigning directions to lanes; flagger means a worker directing traffic through a work zone; flashing arrow panel means a lighted arrow board on a work vehicle showing which lane to use; spur means an interstate branch leading into a city; emergency reference marker means a small mile marker on the interstate shoulder.
Dynamic facts: default and posted speed limits, the interstate minimum speed and work zone fines are set by statute or the highway commission and can change, so posted signs and current law control.
